hypothesis: If hard-shelled eggs are prolate and never oblate spheroids, then essentially every bird egg and every species' mean egg has a length (polar axis) greater than its maximum breadth (equatorial diameter), so L/B > 1.
pass_criterion: Using species-level mean egg length and maximum breadth, the proportion of species with L/B < 1.00 is ≤ 1%, AND no species has mean L/B < 0.95 (beyond about 5% measurement and rounding error).
fail_criterion: More than 1% of species have mean L/B < 1.00, or at least one species with n ≥ 5 eggs has mean L/B < 0.95 that survives a manual check for data-entry errors. Violations that prove to be transcription errors do not count.
interpretation: Thompson's 'prolate spheroid' is a solid of revolution with the polar axis longer than the equatorial axis. 'Oblate/flattened/discoidal' means the polar axis is shorter. Real eggs are asymmetric and not exact spheroids, so the test uses a modern axis-ratio reinterpretation: maximum egg length versus maximum breadth, with L/B > 1 as prolate. The scope is hard-shelled eggs, so it uses birds and not soft-shelled reptile eggs. Exact column names must be confirmed from the dataset README before analysis, because I read the file list but did not open the CSVs.

dataset.name: Data from: The evolution of egg shape in birds: Evolutionary constraints and adaptations
dataset.publisher: Dryad (data by Montgomerie, Birkhead, Thompson and Hemmings)
dataset.why_it_fits: The landing page lists downloadable CSV files, including DATAeggshape.csv (species-level egg shape data) and DATAraweggs.csv (raw egg measurements), plus a README.txt. The egg length and breadth fields, as named in the README, would give L/B per egg and per species. The data cover many bird species, so they test 'never oblate' broadly. I verified the title, authors and file list on the landing page but did not open the CSVs.
